sections.b: Luke sets the coming of the Spirit "as the day of Pentecost came to its fullness" (Acts 2:1), when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims from the Jewish dispersion. The harvest festival becomes the first harvest of the church: about three thousand are added (Acts 2:41). Jubilees already treated the feast as the day of covenant renewal, and the Talmud later calls it the day the Torah was given, so many readers see the giving of the Spirit as a new Sinai, with fire and a sound from heaven (Exodus 19:16–19). Luke does not make the link explicit. Paul later hurries to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost (Acts 20:16) and stays in Ephesus until it (1 Corinthians 16:8).

common: Christians celebrate Pentecost as the birthday of the church, fifty days after Easter.
uncommon: The three thousand saved at Pentecost answer the three thousand who died at Sinai after the golden calf (Exodus 32:28).

sections.h: The Spirit poured out in Acts
sections.b: Acts has been called "the Acts of the Holy Spirit." The risen Jesus gives orders through the Spirit (Acts 1:2), promises power when the Spirit comes (Acts 1:8), and from God's right hand pours out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). Peter reads this as Joel's promise for the last days, for sons and daughters, young and old, slaves (Acts 2:17–18). The Spirit fills believers again for particular tasks, such as Peter before the council (Acts 4:8) and the praying church (Acts 4:31). Christians differ over whether "baptism in the Spirit" is the same as conversion or a later experience; see the card at Acts 2.
sections.refs: Acts 1:2; Acts 1:5–8; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 2:17–18; Acts 2:33; Acts 2:38; Acts 4:8; Acts 4:31; Joel 2:28–32

common: The Spirit came for the first time at Pentecost.
Being filled with the Spirit always shows itself by speaking in tongues.
uncommon: Pentecost answers Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29).

sections.b: At Pentecost the believers speak "in other languages as the Spirit gave them words to declare" (Acts 2:4), and pilgrims from about fifteen lands hear God's great deeds in their own native languages (Acts 2:8–11). The Greek word glōssa means both the tongue and a language, and the "tongues like fire" of Acts 2:3 use the same word. Some hearers mock them as drunk (Acts 2:13), which suggests that not everyone understood. Readers debate whether this was the same gift Paul regulates at Corinth, which needed an interpreter (1 Corinthians 14:27–28).

common: The tongues at Pentecost were the same as the tongues in Corinth.
uncommon: The miracle at Pentecost was in the hearing, not in the speaking.

common: Jesus ascended on Easter evening, as Luke 24 seems to say.
uncommon: The forty days of Acts 1:3 are a symbolic number, not a count of days.

common: Acts records everything the apostles did.
uncommon: Luke planned a third volume, since he calls his Gospel the "first" book (Acts 1:1).

sections.b: In a parenthesis within Peter's speech, Luke tells that Judas came to own a piece of land with the pay for his wrongdoing, fell headlong and burst open, so that the place was called Akeldama, Field of Blood (Acts 1:18–19). Matthew says instead that Judas returned the silver and hanged himself, and that the priests bought the field (Matthew 27:3–10). Peter applies Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8 to him: his place is left empty, and another takes his charge (Acts 1:20). The Twelve are restored by the choice of Matthias, and Judas is said to have gone "to his own place" (Acts 1:25).

common: Judas hanged himself, and the rope broke.
uncommon: Judas' bursting open echoes the death of the wicked in Wisdom of Solomon 4:19.

sections.b: Acts lists the eleven apostles by name (Acts 1:13), then tells how Matthias was chosen to bring them back to twelve before Pentecost (Acts 1:15–26). Peter's requirement, a witness who had been with Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension (Acts 1:21–22), defines the Twelve as eyewitnesses of the resurrection. Their number stands for Israel's twelve tribes (Luke 22:30), and once complete they speak to "the whole house of Israel" (Acts 2:14, 36). The apostles teach (Acts 2:42), do signs (Acts 2:43), receive the community's gifts (Acts 4:35), and are tried before the council (Acts 4:5–21).

common: The apostles chose Matthias by mistake, and Paul was God's real choice.
uncommon: The 120 of Acts 1:15 is ten for each of the Twelve, a community large enough to have its own council.

sections.h: The last lot in the Bible
sections.b: The believers put forward two men, pray to the Lord who knows every heart, and cast lots; the lot falls on Matthias (Acts 1:23–26). It is the last time Scripture shows God's people deciding by lot. After Pentecost, Acts shows decisions made by the Spirit's guidance, prayer and the church's discussion (Acts 6:3–6; 13:2; 15:28).

At Babel God mixed up the language of all the earth and scattered the nations (Genesis 11:7–9). At Pentecost a crowd from every nation is "thrown into confusion" (Acts 2:6), Luke's word being the verb the Greek Old Testament uses at Babel, because each hears the believers in his own language. From the church fathers on, many have read Pentecost as Babel reversed: the Spirit gathers what pride scattered, and God's praise is understood in every tongue. Luke does not say so in so many words; the reading is an old interpretation.

uncommon: The list of nations in Acts 2:9–11 is a deliberate echo of the table of nations in Genesis 10.

sections.b: Luke lists Jews and converts from Parthia, Media, Elam and Mesopotamia in the east, through Judea, Asia Minor, Egypt and Libya, to Rome, Crete and Arabia (Acts 2:9–11). The list moves roughly from east to west and covers the lands of the Jewish dispersion. Readers have compared it with the table of the nations in Genesis 10, with Philo's list of Jewish settlements, and with an ancient astrological list of lands. Its message is that the whole known world was represented at the church's birth, in the persons of Israel's scattered children.

Peter's answer to the crowd, "Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38), is the first Christian call to baptism in Acts, and about three thousand are baptized that day (Acts 2:41). The verse joins repentance, baptism, Jesus' name, forgiveness and the Spirit, and Christians still differ over how these are related, whether baptism brings forgiveness or signifies it, and whether "your children" (Acts 2:39) includes infants. See the card at Acts 2 and the card at Matthew 28:19 on the formula.

common: Acts 2:38 gives the words that must be said at every baptism.
uncommon: "For the forgiveness of sins" means "because your sins have been forgiven."

sections.h: "Will you restore the kingdom to Israel?"
sections.b: The apostles' last question to the risen Jesus is about Israel's kingdom (Acts 1:6). Jesus answers only that the timing belongs to the Father, and gives them a mission to the end of the earth (Acts 1:7–8). Peter later tells the people of Jerusalem that if they repent, times of relief will come and God will send the Messiah, who must remain in heaven until "the restoring of all things" (Acts 3:19–21), and that God sent his servant "for you first" (Acts 3:26). Interpreters disagree whether Acts keeps a future for national Israel (Jervell, dispensationalists) or sees the promise fulfilled in the church of Jews and Gentiles.

Twice Luke describes the first believers holding their goods in common: they sold land and possessions and gave to anyone in need (Acts 2:44–45), and "Nobody among them was in need" (Acts 4:34), as Deuteronomy 15:4 promised. Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:36–37). Peter tells the lame man he has no silver or gold (Acts 3:6). The sharing was voluntary (Acts 5:4), and Christians have read it as a model for monasteries and communities such as the Hutterites, as an ideal of generosity for all, or as a short-lived experiment; see the card at Acts 4.

common: The early church practiced a form of communism.
uncommon: The Jerusalem church ran a formal common fund on the Essene model.

sections.b: In his speech in Solomon's Porch Peter quotes Moses' promise, "From among your brothers the Lord God will raise up a prophet for you, a prophet like me," and warns, in words taken from Leviticus 23:29, that everyone who will not listen will be wiped out from the people (Acts 3:22–23). He presents Jesus as that prophet, raised up first for Israel (Acts 3:26). Stephen quotes the same promise (Acts 7:37).

Peter's speech and the church's prayer call Jesus God's "servant" (pais): God "has given glory to his servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13), raised him up for Israel first (Acts 3:26), and anointed "your holy servant" (Acts 4:27, 30). The words echo Isaiah 52:13 in the Greek, where the servant is "lifted up and glorified," and Isaiah 53, the servant who suffers. The KJV's "Son" or "child" Jesus hides this link. The title is one of the earliest names for Jesus and later fell out of use.

sections.h: The first believers at the temple
sections.b: The Jerusalem believers met daily in the temple courts (Acts 2:46). Peter and John went up at the afternoon hour of prayer, healed a lame man at the gate called Beautiful, and preached in Solomon's Porch (Acts 3:1–11). Their arrest came from the priests, the commander of the temple and the Sadducees (Acts 4:1). Acts shows the movement as faithful Jews worshiping in Israel's sanctuary, not yet a separate religion.

Peter tells the people of Jerusalem that they handed Jesus over and, using men outside the law, killed him (Acts 2:23, 36; 3:13–15; 4:10). These are a Jewish apostle's words to fellow Jews of Jerusalem a few weeks after the event, meant to bring them to repentance, and they come with forgiveness offered and the admission that "you did not understand what you were doing" (Acts 3:17). Later Christians turned such verses into a charge against all Jews of all times. The Second Vatican Council rejected that reading (Nostra Aetate 4), and so do most churches today.

sections.h: "This same Jesus ... will come this same way"
sections.b: At the ascension two men in white promise the watching apostles that "this same Jesus, taken up from you into the sky, will come this same way, just as you watched him go into the sky" (Acts 1:11). Peter later speaks of God sending Jesus, the appointed Messiah, after "times of relief" when heaven no longer holds him (Acts 3:19–21). Acts gives no timetable: "Knowing the times or the seasons does not belong to you" (Acts 1:7).

Peter changes Joel's "after these things" to "in the last days" (Acts 2:17) and says the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost is the fulfillment. For Acts, the last days began with Jesus' resurrection and the gift of the Spirit, and they last until "the day of the Lord comes, that great and shining day" (Acts 2:20).

sections.h: The Psalms in the first sermons
sections.b: Peter's early speeches lean on the Psalms, read as prophecy spoken by the Spirit "through the mouth of David" (Acts 1:16; 4:25): Psalms 69 and 109 for Judas (Acts 1:20), Psalm 16 for the resurrection (Acts 2:25–28), Psalm 110 for the ascension (Acts 2:34–35), Psalm 118 for the rejected stone (Acts 4:11) and Psalm 2 for the plot against God's anointed (Acts 4:25–26). Peter usually follows the Greek translation, which sometimes changes the sense, as with "hope" and "decay" in Psalm 16.
sections.refs: Acts 1:20; Acts 2:25–35; Acts 4:11; Acts 4:25–26; Psalm 2:1–2; Psalm 16:8–11; Psalm 110:1; Psalm 118:22

sections.b: Peter's Pentecost sermon ends with the claim that God has made the crucified Jesus "both Lord and Messiah" (Acts 2:36). In Solomon's Porch he says God foretold that "his Messiah was to suffer" (Acts 3:18) and will send "Jesus, the Messiah he chose ahead of time" (Acts 3:20); the church's prayer applies Psalm 2's "his anointed" to Jesus (Acts 4:26–27). Readers debate whether "made" reflects an early belief that Jesus became Messiah at his resurrection, or means that God publicly installed him as what he already was.
sections.refs: Acts 2:31; Acts 2:36; Acts 3:18–20; Acts 4:26–27; Luke 2:11; Psalm 2:2

sections.h: The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
sections.b: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth "in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene" (Acts 3:6). He leaps and walks into the temple, recalling Isaiah's promise that the lame will leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6). Peter insists that the healing came not from his own power or godliness but from faith in Jesus' name (Acts 3:12, 16), and before the council he uses the verb "saved" for the healing (Acts 4:9) to lead into salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12).

Before the Sanhedrin Peter applies Psalm 118:22 directly to his judges: Jesus is "the stone that you, the builders, treated as nothing" (Acts 4:11). He uses a stronger verb than the Greek Psalm, "count as nothing," and turns the quotation into a charge. Jesus had used the same verse against the chief priests (Luke 20:17), and 1 Peter 2:7 repeats it.

The disciple who denied Jesus three times now leads the community: he explains Judas' fall and proposes a successor (Acts 1:15–22), preaches at Pentecost (Acts 2:14–40), heals the lame man (Acts 3:6–7), preaches again in the temple (Acts 3:12–26) and defends the faith before the council (Acts 4:8–20). The council notices that he and John have had no schooling, and that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13).

sections.h: The brothers in the upper room
sections.b: After the ascension Jesus' brothers pray with the apostles and with Mary (Acts 1:14). During his ministry they had not believed in him (John 7:5); Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), who later leads the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13).

sections.h: "Is it right before God to heed you?"
sections.b: Ordered by the Sanhedrin to stop speaking in Jesus' name, Peter and John answer, "Is it right before God to heed you rather than God? Decide for yourselves" (Acts 4:19), a principle repeated in Acts 5:29. Their refusal is respectful and public, and they accept the consequences. The words echo Socrates before his judges and the Maccabean martyrs, and have been cited by Christians resisting unjust commands ever since.
